elements: Defendant drove a motor vehicle in South Carolina
While driving, defendant was under the influence of alcohol, drugs, or a combination
Defendant's faculties to drive were materially and appreciably impaired, OR defendant had a BAC of .08 or higher
mandatory_minimum: 48 hours or 48 hours community service (first); 5 days (second); 60 days (third); 1 year (fourth+)
enhancements: BAC .16 or higher (most severe penalty tier)
Great bodily injury or death (felony DUI under § 56-5-2945)
notes: SC uses a tiered BAC penalty structure: .08-.10, .10-.16, and .16+. Implied consent under § 56-5-2950. Administrative license suspension separate from criminal penalties. Ignition interlock device (IID) may be required. SC eliminated provisional license in 2014 — IID is the primary restricted driving option.

statute_title: Driving Under the Influence — First Offense
elements: Defendant drove a motor vehicle in South Carolina
While driving, defendant was under the influence of alcohol, drugs, or a combination
Defendant's faculties to drive were materially and appreciably impaired OR BAC .08 or higher
No prior DUI convictions within 10 years
mandatory_minimum: 48 hours imprisonment or 48 hours community service
enhancements: BAC .10 to .16 (increased mandatory minimum and fine)
BAC .16 or higher (72 hours mandatory minimum, higher fine)
notes: License suspension 6 months. Enrollment in ADSAP (Alcohol and Drug Safety Action Program) required. Temporary alcohol license available after 30 days if enrolled in ADSAP. IID may be installed in lieu of full suspension.

statute_title: Driving Under the Influence — Second Offense
elements: Defendant drove a motor vehicle in South Carolina
While driving, defendant was under the influence
Faculties materially and appreciably impaired OR BAC .08 or higher
One prior DUI conviction within 10 years
notes: License suspension 1 year. IID required for 2 years after suspension period. ADSAP enrollment mandatory. Vehicle may be immobilized or impounded.

statute_title: Driving Under the Influence — Third Offense
elements: Defendant drove a motor vehicle in South Carolina
While driving, defendant was under the influence
Faculties materially and appreciably impaired OR BAC .08 or higher
Two prior DUI convictions within 10 years
enhancements: BAC .10 to .16 (increased mandatory minimum and fine)
notes: License suspension 2 years minimum. Permanent revocation possible. IID required for 3 years after reinstatement. Vehicle may be confiscated. ADSAP completion mandatory.

statute_title: Driving Under the Influence — Fourth or Subsequent Offense
elements: Defendant drove a motor vehicle in South Carolina
While driving, defendant was under the influence
Faculties materially and appreciably impaired OR BAC .08 or higher
Three or more prior DUI convictions
notes: Permanent license revocation. No provisional license available. Vehicle subject to forfeiture. No parole or suspended sentence for mandatory minimum.

penalty_max: Same as alcohol DUI based on number of offenses
fine_max: Same as alcohol DUI based on number of offenses
elements: Defendant drove a motor vehicle in South Carolina
While driving, defendant was under the influence of any drug or combination of drugs
Defendant's faculties to drive were materially and appreciably impaired
enhancements: Prior DUI convictions (same escalation as alcohol DUI)
notes: SC has no per se drug impairment limit. BAC tiers do not apply to drug-only DUI — prosecution must prove impairment. Urine and blood testing used. Drug Recognition Expert (DRE) evaluations are admissible. Implied consent applies to blood and urine for drugs.

statute_title: Felony Driving Under the Influence Resulting in Great Bodily Injury or Death
elements: Defendant drove a motor vehicle in South Carolina while under the influence
As a proximate result, the defendant caused great bodily injury or death to another person
Great bodily injury means injury creating a substantial risk of death, serious permanent disfigurement, or protracted loss of function
enhancements: Death of victim (mandatory minimum 1 year, up to 25 years)
notes: This is a standalone felony, not an enhancement to § 56-5-2930. Conviction carries mandatory license revocation. No suspended sentence or probation on the mandatory minimum. Restitution to victims is standard.

statute_title: Child Endangerment — DUI With Minor Passenger
offense_class: Misdemeanor (additional penalty on top of DUI)
elements: Defendant was driving under the influence per § 56-5-2930
A minor under age 16 was a passenger in the vehicle at the time
notes: SC law § 56-5-2947 provides additional penalties for DUI with a child passenger under 16. This is charged in addition to the underlying DUI charge, not as a standalone offense.

elements: Defendant drove a vehicle in South Carolina
Defendant drove in willful or wanton disregard for the safety of persons or property
enhancements: Third or subsequent offense (up to 1 year)
notes: Commonly used as a plea-down from DUI. Points assessed on driving record. License suspension possible for repeat offenders. Often charged alongside other traffic offenses.

statute_title: Duty to Stop When Involved in Accident — Property Damage
elements: Defendant was the driver of a vehicle involved in an accident
The accident resulted in damage to a vehicle or other property
Defendant failed to stop at the scene or as close thereto as possible
Defendant failed to provide name, address, registration, and license information
notes: Property-damage-only hit and run. Must provide information to other driver or report to law enforcement if other driver is not present.

statute_title: Duty to Stop When Involved in Accident — Personal Injury or Death
elements: Defendant was the driver of a vehicle involved in an accident
The accident resulted in injury or death to another person
Defendant knew or should have known that injury or death resulted
Defendant failed to stop and render aid or provide information
notes: Significant felony penalties. Leaving the scene of an accident involving death carries penalties nearly as severe as vehicular homicide. Driver must provide reasonable assistance to injured persons.

elements: Defendant drove a motor vehicle while under the influence of alcohol, drugs, or both
As a proximate result, the defendant caused the death of another person
notes: SC does not have a general 'vehicular homicide' statute separate from DUI death. Non-DUI vehicular deaths are prosecuted under reckless homicide § 56-5-2910 or involuntary manslaughter. This statute specifically addresses DUI-caused deaths.

elements: Defendant drove a motor vehicle in South Carolina
Defendant drove in a reckless manner
As a proximate result, the defendant caused the death of another person
enhancements: Gross intoxication at time of accident
notes: SC calls this 'reckless homicide' rather than vehicular manslaughter. Covers non-DUI reckless driving deaths. DUI-related deaths are charged under § 56-5-2945 (felony DUI death) which carries heavier penalties.

penalty_max: 30 days or $300 fine (first); 60 days or $600 fine (second); 90 days or $900 fine (third+)
elements: Defendant drove a motor vehicle on a public road in South Carolina
At the time, defendant's license was suspended or revoked
Defendant had knowledge of the suspension or revocation
enhancements: Driving under DUI suspension (§ 56-1-460(A)(2) — harsher penalties)
notes: Driving under DUI suspension carries stricter penalties than general suspension. § 56-1-460(A)(2) applies when suspension resulted from DUI. Habitual offender status (§ 56-1-1020) possible after 3 suspensions in 3 years.

statute_title: Failure to Stop for Blue Light
offense_class: Misdemeanor (no injury); Felony (with injury/death or 200+ mph chase)
elements: A law enforcement vehicle gave a signal to stop by blue light and siren
Defendant was the driver of the pursued vehicle
Defendant willfully failed to stop or attempted to elude the officer
Defendant increased speed or extinguished lights to elude
enhancements: Great bodily injury to another during pursuit (felony, up to 10 years)
Death of another during pursuit (felony, up to 25 years)
Speeds exceeding posted limit by 35 mph or more
notes: SC calls this 'failure to stop for blue light.' Creating a risk of injury to others during pursuit elevates the offense. Officers must be in marked patrol vehicles or clearly identifiable. Conviction carries license suspension.

elements: Defendant operated a motor vehicle on a public road in South Carolina
Defendant engaged in a race, speed competition, or drag race with another vehicle
notes: License suspension mandatory. Applies to both organized and spontaneous street racing. Can be charged alongside reckless driving.

elements: Defendant transported an open container of beer, wine, or liquor in a motor vehicle
The container was in the passenger area of the vehicle
The seal was broken or the contents partially removed
notes: SC open container law applies to drivers and passengers. Trunk or locked glove compartment storage is exempt. Does not apply to the living quarters of a motor home. Often charged alongside DUI.

statute_title: Implied Consent — Refusal of Chemical Test
offense_class: Administrative (civil license suspension), not a criminal offense
penalty_max: License suspension only (no criminal penalty for refusal itself)
elements: Defendant was arrested for DUI or had involvement in a traffic incident resulting in death or injury
Law enforcement requested a chemical test of blood, breath, or urine
Defendant refused to submit to the requested test
enhancements: Prior refusals (9-month suspension for second; 12-month for third+)
notes: Refusal triggers a 6-month administrative license suspension (first offense). Refusal is admissible as evidence at trial. Defendant has right to an administrative hearing within 30 days. SC does not criminalize refusal itself, but it results in automatic suspension and can be used as evidence of consciousness of guilt.

statute_title: Simple Possession of a Controlled Substance
penalty_max: 6 months or $1,000 fine (first); 1 year or $2,000 fine (second); 2 years or $5,000 fine (third+)
elements: Defendant knowingly or intentionally possessed a controlled substance
The substance is listed in SC Controlled Substances schedules (§ 44-53-190 through 44-53-270)
Defendant did not have a valid prescription for the substance
enhancements: Third or subsequent offense (up to 2 years, $5,000 fine)
notes: Simple possession is charged under § 44-53-370(d). SC Controlled Substances Act mirrors federal scheduling. Conditional discharge (PTI) available for first offense — charges dismissed upon completion. Drug court diversion may be available.

elements: Defendant knowingly or intentionally possessed marijuana
The amount was for personal use (1 ounce or less for lowest tier)
enhancements: Possession of more than 1 ounce (charged as regular controlled substance possession)
Second or subsequent offense (up to 1 year)
notes: SC has no medical or recreational marijuana legalization. First-offense possession of 1 oz or less is a lesser misdemeanor (30 days/$200). Conditional discharge available for first offense. Hash/concentrates are charged under the general drug schedule, not the marijuana provision.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (simple possession); Felony (possession with intent/trafficking thresholds)
penalty_max: 2 years (simple possession, first); 5 years (second); trafficking thresholds apply at 10g+
elements: Defendant knowingly or intentionally possessed cocaine (Schedule II)
Defendant did not have a lawful prescription or authority
enhancements: Trafficking amount (10g-28g: 3-10 years mandatory; 28g-100g: 7-25 years mandatory; 100g-200g: 25 years mandatory; 200g-400g: 25 years mandatory; 400g+: 25-30 years mandatory)
Proximity to school, park, or church
notes: Cocaine is Schedule II in SC. Trafficking thresholds under § 44-53-370(e) are triggered at 10 grams. Crack and powder cocaine are treated identically under SC law. Mandatory minimums for trafficking are severe and non-suspendable.

offense_class: Felony (any amount for trafficking; Misdemeanor for simple possession under § 44-53-370(d))
penalty_max: 2 years (simple possession); trafficking: 3-25 years depending on amount
elements: Defendant knowingly or intentionally possessed methamphetamine
Defendant did not have lawful authority
enhancements: Trafficking amounts (10g+ triggers mandatory minimums under § 44-53-375)
notes: SC has a specific methamphetamine trafficking statute (§ 44-53-375) with severe mandatory minimums. Simple possession (below trafficking thresholds) is charged under § 44-53-370(d). Manufacturing carries separate penalties. Pseudoephedrine purchase restrictions under § 44-53-398.

elements: Defendant knowingly or intentionally possessed an opioid (heroin, fentanyl, oxycodone, etc.)
The substance is listed in Schedule I or II
Defendant did not have a valid prescription
enhancements: Fentanyl presence (treated as heroin equivalent for scheduling)
notes: Heroin trafficking thresholds in SC are very low — 4 grams triggers mandatory minimum of 7 years. Fentanyl is scheduled as a narcotic. Prescription opioids without a valid Rx fall under simple possession or trafficking depending on amount. SC has adopted analogue act provisions for fentanyl variants.

statute_title: Possession of Prescription Drugs Without a Valid Prescription
elements: Defendant possessed a prescription drug listed in the controlled substances schedules
Defendant did not have a valid prescription from an authorized prescriber
Defendant knew or should have known the nature of the substance
enhancements: Possession of large quantities (may trigger intent to distribute)
notes: Common prescription drugs charged: benzodiazepines (Xanax), opioids (oxycodone, hydrocodone), stimulants (Adderall). Conditional discharge available for first offense. Obtaining prescriptions by fraud is a separate felony under § 44-53-390.

elements: Defendant knowingly sold, manufactured, delivered, purchased, or possessed a controlled substance
The quantity met or exceeded the statutory trafficking threshold for that substance
mandatory_minimum: Varies by substance and weight — cocaine 10g+: 3 years; heroin 4g+: 7 years; marijuana 10 lbs+: 1 year; meth 10g+: 3 years
enhancements: Higher weight tiers carry progressively longer mandatory minimums
Trafficking near schools, parks, or churches
notes: SC trafficking statutes carry some of the harshest mandatory minimums in the country. Sentences are non-suspendable and non-paroleable for the mandatory portion. Substantial assistance to law enforcement (§ 44-53-420) is the primary mechanism to reduce mandatory minimums. Thresholds: marijuana 10 lbs; cocaine 10g; heroin 4g; meth 10g; LSD 100 dosage units.

penalty_max: 5 years (Schedule III-V, first); 15 years (Schedule I/II narcotics, first); doubles on second+
fine_max: $5,000 (Schedule III-V); no statutory cap for Schedule I/II
elements: Defendant manufactured, distributed, dispensed, or possessed with intent to distribute
The substance was a controlled substance listed in SC schedules
Defendant acted knowingly or intentionally
enhancements: Distribution within proximity of a school (§ 44-53-445)
Use of a firearm during offense
notes: Penalties depend on the schedule of the substance. Schedule I/II narcotics carry the heaviest penalties. Distribution near a school zone (within 1/2 mile) triggers additional penalties under § 44-53-445. Second offense mandatory minimum for Schedule I/II narcotics.

elements: Defendant manufactured or created a controlled substance
The substance is listed in SC Controlled Substances schedules
Defendant acted knowingly or intentionally
enhancements: Manufacturing methamphetamine (separate statute § 44-53-375(B) with harsher penalties)
notes: Methamphetamine manufacturing carries enhanced penalties under § 44-53-375(B). Growing marijuana is manufacturing. Clandestine lab cleanup costs may be assessed. Child endangerment charges added if minors present.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (civil fine for possession; criminal for sale/delivery)
elements: Defendant possessed drug paraphernalia
The paraphernalia was used or intended for use in introducing a controlled substance into the body, or for manufacturing, packaging, or distributing
enhancements: Sale or delivery of paraphernalia to a minor (enhanced penalty)
Delivery to person under 18 who is at least 3 years younger
notes: SC § 44-53-391 distinguishes between use/possession paraphernalia and sale/delivery paraphernalia. Items considered include pipes, rolling papers, scales, baggies. Context determines whether an item is paraphernalia.

elements: Defendant obtained or attempted to obtain a controlled substance by fraud, deceit, misrepresentation, or subterfuge
This includes forging prescriptions, doctor shopping, or providing false information
notes: Covers doctor shopping, forged prescriptions, altered prescriptions, and impersonation. SC Prescription Monitoring Program (PMP) data is used to detect doctor shopping. Each fraudulent prescription may constitute a separate offense.

fine_max: $5,000 (Schedule III-V); statutory maximum for Schedule I/II
elements: Defendant possessed a controlled substance
Defendant intended to distribute the substance
Intent may be inferred from quantity, packaging, presence of scales, cash, or other indicia of distribution
notes: Intent to distribute is often proven through circumstantial evidence: quantity beyond personal use, packaging materials, scales, large amounts of cash, pay/owe sheets. No statutory threshold — jury determines intent. Charged under same statute as distribution.

penalty_max: Same as the underlying drug offense
fine_max: Same as the underlying drug offense
elements: An agreement existed between two or more persons to violate the SC Controlled Substances Act
Defendant knowingly and voluntarily joined the conspiracy
An overt act was committed in furtherance of the conspiracy
enhancements: Conspiracy to traffic (triggers trafficking mandatory minimums)
notes: Drug conspiracy in SC carries the same penalties as the underlying offense. Trafficking conspiracy triggers trafficking mandatory minimums. Each co-conspirator can be held liable for the reasonably foreseeable acts of others in the conspiracy.

offense_class: Felony (Capital — death or life without parole)
penalty_max: Death or life imprisonment without parole
elements: Defendant caused the death of another person
The killing was committed with malice aforethought
At least one statutory aggravating circumstance exists (for death penalty eligibility)
mandatory_minimum: 30 years (if death penalty not sought); life without parole (if statutory aggravators found)
enhancements: Statutory aggravating circumstances (§ 16-3-20(C)) including: during commission of another felony, prior murder conviction, victim was law enforcement, multiple victims, kidnapping
notes: SC does not label murder as 'first degree' or 'second degree.' Murder under § 16-3-20 is the killing of a person with malice aforethought. The death penalty is available when statutory aggravating circumstances are found beyond a reasonable doubt. SC reinstated the firing squad as an execution method in 2023. Life without parole is mandatory minimum when aggravators are found but death is not imposed.

elements: Defendant caused the death of another person
The killing was committed with malice aforethought
No statutory aggravating circumstances apply
notes: SC treats all murder as a single offense under § 16-3-20 — there is no statutory first/second degree distinction. The presence or absence of aggravating factors determines sentencing range (death-eligible vs. 30-to-life). This entry covers murder without death-penalty-qualifying aggravators.

elements: Defendant caused the death of another person
The killing was committed in the sudden heat of passion upon sufficient legal provocation
There was no premeditation or malice aforethought
notes: Voluntary manslaughter is a lesser included offense of murder. Provocation must be legally sufficient — words alone generally do not qualify. The time between provocation and killing must not be long enough for a reasonable person to cool off.

elements: Defendant caused the death of another person
The death resulted from the defendant's criminal negligence or reckless disregard for the safety of others
The defendant did not intend to kill
notes: Involuntary manslaughter requires criminal negligence — ordinary negligence is insufficient. Commonly charged in cases of accidental shooting deaths, workplace deaths, or non-DUI vehicle deaths where reckless homicide does not apply.

elements: Defendant performed an act with the specific intent to kill another person
The act went beyond mere preparation toward commission of murder
The intended victim survived
enhancements: Victim was a law enforcement officer or public official
notes: SC has a specific attempted murder statute (§ 16-3-29) enacted in 2010. Prior to this, attempted murder was charged under the general attempt statute. Maximum 30 years imprisonment.

statute_title: Assault and Battery in the First Degree
elements: Defendant unlawfully injured another person
The injury involved great bodily injury, OR
The injury was committed during the commission of a robbery, burglary, kidnapping, or theft, OR
The injury could have reasonably resulted in death
enhancements: Use of a deadly weapon (may be charged under ABHAN instead)
Victim was a first responder or public official
notes: SC reformed its assault/battery laws in 2012. The old common-law 'aggravated assault' was replaced by the statutory three-degree system under § 16-3-600. First degree (most serious) is a felony with up to 10 years.

statute_title: Assault and Battery in the Third Degree
elements: Defendant unlawfully injured another person, OR
Defendant offered or attempted to injure another person with the present ability to do so
notes: Third degree is the lowest level — equivalent to simple assault/battery. SC merged assault and battery into a single statutory scheme in 2012 under § 16-3-600. No separate 'assault' vs 'battery' distinction.

statute_title: Assault and Battery in the Second Degree
elements: Defendant unlawfully injured another person and the injury was moderate bodily injury, OR
Defendant injured another during the commission of a crime not otherwise covered by first degree, OR
The victim was a protected class (school employee in performance of duties, etc.)
enhancements: Moderate bodily injury (injury requiring medical treatment but not constituting great bodily injury)
notes: Second degree fills the middle ground between third degree (minor) and first degree (great bodily injury). SC does not have a separate 'battery' statute — this is the closest equivalent. Moderate bodily injury is the key distinguishing factor.

statute_title: Assault and Battery in the First Degree (Great Bodily Injury)
elements: Defendant unlawfully injured another person
The injury constituted great bodily injury (substantial risk of death, serious permanent disfigurement, or protracted loss of a bodily member or organ)
notes: Same statute as aggravated assault — SC's first-degree A&B covers what other states separate into aggravated assault and aggravated battery. 'Great bodily injury' is the statutory trigger.

statute_title: Assault and Battery of a High and Aggravated Nature (ABHAN)
elements: Defendant unlawfully injured or attempted to injure another person
The act was accomplished by means likely to produce death or great bodily injury, OR
The act involved non-consensual touching of the private parts of a person under 16
notes: ABHAN (Assault and Battery of a High and Aggravated Nature) is SC's equivalent of assault with a deadly weapon or assault with intent to kill. It sits above first-degree A&B in severity (20 years max vs. 10 years). Common in cases involving weapons, strangulation, or extreme violence.

statute_title: Assault and Battery of a High and Aggravated Nature — With Firearm
elements: Defendant committed an assault and battery using a firearm
The act was by means likely to produce death or great bodily injury
enhancements: Pointing a firearm at another (may be charged separately under § 16-23-410)
notes: Charged as ABHAN when a firearm is used. Pointing a firearm at another person is a separate misdemeanor under § 16-23-410 (up to 5 years or $1,000 fine). Using a firearm during the commission of a violent crime triggers additional penalties.

statute_title: Assault and Battery in the First Degree — Against Law Enforcement
elements: Defendant unlawfully injured a law enforcement officer
The officer was performing official duties at the time
Defendant knew or should have known the victim was a law enforcement officer
notes: Assaulting a law enforcement officer automatically elevates the charge to first-degree A&B under SC law. Separate from the general resisting arrest statute. Also applies to firefighters, EMS, and other specified public safety personnel.

elements: Defendant took personal property from the person or presence of another
The taking was by violence or intimidation
Defendant intended to permanently deprive the victim of the property
enhancements: Use of a deadly weapon (armed robbery under § 16-11-330)
notes: Common-law robbery codified in SC. No minimum mandatory sentence for simple robbery. Distinguished from armed robbery by absence of a weapon. Larceny from a person without force or intimidation is a separate lesser offense.

elements: Defendant took personal property from the person or presence of another
The taking was by violence or intimidation
Defendant was armed with a deadly weapon or an alleged deadly weapon at the time
mandatory_minimum: 10 years (no parole, probation, or suspended sentence)
enhancements: Use of a firearm during robbery
notes: Armed robbery carries a harsh 10-year mandatory minimum that cannot be suspended. An 'alleged' deadly weapon (even a toy gun represented as real) qualifies. No parole on mandatory portion. This is one of SC's most severely punished property crimes.

elements: Defendant unlawfully seized, confined, inveigled, decoyed, kidnapped, abducted, or carried away another person
The act was done by any means whatsoever without authority of law
notes: SC's broad kidnapping statute covers any unlawful seizure or confinement. No requirement of movement (asportation) — confinement alone is sufficient. When combined with other felonies, may trigger murder aggravating circumstances.

statute_title: Arson — First, Second, and Third Degree
penalty_max: 25 years (first degree — dwelling); 15 years (second degree — insured property); 5 years (third degree — other property)
elements: Defendant willfully and maliciously set fire to or caused an explosion that damaged or destroyed a building or structure
First degree: the building was a dwelling and a person was in or near it
Second degree: the building was insured and the act was intended to defraud
Third degree: any other building or property
enhancements: First degree — person present in dwelling (up to 25 years)
Injury or death resulting from arson
notes: SC has three degrees of arson. First degree (dwelling with person present) is the most serious. Arson of a church or place of worship is charged under § 16-11-110(A) with up to 25 years. Attempted arson is a separate offense.

elements: Defendant took or attempted to take a motor vehicle from another person
The taking was by force or intimidation or threat of force
The vehicle was in the immediate presence of the person
notes: SC enacted a specific carjacking statute. Distinguished from armed robbery by the specific targeting of a motor vehicle. Can be charged alongside armed robbery.

statute_title: Threatening Life, Person, or Family of Public Official or Employee
elements: Defendant conveyed a threat to take the life of or inflict bodily harm upon a public official, public employee, or a member of their family
The threat was made willfully
notes: SC does not have a general 'terroristic threats' statute. Threats against public officials are covered under § 16-3-1040. General threats of violence are typically charged as criminal threats/intimidation under § 16-3-620 or ABHAN depending on circumstances.

elements: Defendant unlawfully confined another person
The confinement was without lawful authority or consent
notes: SC does not have a separate 'unlawful imprisonment' or 'false imprisonment' statute. Unlawful confinement is charged under the kidnapping statute (§ 16-3-910). Defense may argue for lesser-included offense treatment at sentencing.

elements: Defendant entered a dwelling without consent
The dwelling was occupied at the time
Defendant had the intent to commit a crime therein
At least one aggravating circumstance: armed with a deadly weapon, caused physical injury, used threats, or the act occurred during the night
mandatory_minimum: 15 years (no parole, probation, or suspended sentence)
enhancements: Armed with a deadly weapon during entry
notes: SC's first-degree burglary is functionally equivalent to 'home invasion.' The 15-year mandatory minimum is non-suspendable. This is one of SC's most severely punished offenses. Night-time entry of an occupied dwelling with any aggravating factor triggers first degree.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (under general extortion); Felony (under specific statutes)
elements: Defendant attempted to obtain something of value from another person
By means of threat, intimidation, or coercion
The threat related to causing harm, damaging reputation, or revealing information
notes: SC's extortion/blackmail statute (§ 16-17-640) is a common-law based misdemeanor. More serious extortion cases may be charged under conspiracy, kidnapping, or other applicable felony statutes depending on the nature of the threat.

penalty_max: 30 days (petit larceny); 5 years (grand larceny $2,001-$10,000); 10 years (grand larceny $10,000+)
elements: Defendant took and carried away the personal property of another
Without the owner's consent
With the intent to permanently deprive the owner of the property
enhancements: Value over $10,000 (enhanced grand larceny — up to 10 years)
Theft from a person (larceny from person under § 16-13-150)
notes: SC uses the $2,000 threshold for grand vs. petit larceny. The threshold was raised from $1,000 to $2,000 in 2010. Grand larceny over $10,000 carries enhanced penalties. SC merged several forms of theft under § 16-13-30.

elements: Defendant took and carried away the personal property of another
The value of the property exceeded $2,000
Without the owner's consent and with intent to permanently deprive
notes: Grand larceny threshold in SC is $2,000. Two tiers: $2,001-$10,000 (up to 5 years) and $10,000+ (up to 10 years). Restitution is standard.

elements: Defendant took and carried away the personal property of another
The value of the property was $2,000 or less
Without the owner's consent and with intent to permanently deprive
notes: Petit larceny in SC is a misdemeanor with up to 30 days imprisonment. No fine specified by statute — judge's discretion. Conditional discharge may be available for first offense.

elements: Defendant took merchandise from a retail establishment
Without paying the full purchase price
With the intent to deprive the merchant of possession or value
This includes altering price tags, transferring goods between containers, or concealment
enhancements: Second offense ($2,000 or less — up to 30 days, $500 fine, and community service)
Third or subsequent ($2,000 or less — up to 90 days or $500 fine)
notes: SC shoplifting statute covers concealment, altering price tags, transferring between containers, and under-ringing. Merchants have a right to detain suspected shoplifters (§ 16-13-140). Enhanced penalties for repeat offenders.

elements: Defendant entered a dwelling without consent
With the intent to commit a crime therein
No aggravating circumstance of first-degree burglary present (not armed, no injury, no threats, not at night or with occupants)
enhancements: Presence of aggravating circumstances (elevates to first degree)
notes: Second-degree burglary applies to entry into a dwelling without the aggravating factors that trigger first degree. SC has a three-degree burglary system: first degree (dwelling + aggravators), second degree (dwelling without aggravators), third degree (non-dwelling buildings).

elements: Defendant entered a dwelling without consent
With the intent to commit a crime therein
At least one aggravating circumstance: armed with a deadly weapon, caused physical injury, used threats of force, or entered during the night while the dwelling was occupied
mandatory_minimum: 15 years (no probation, parole, or suspended sentence)
notes: First-degree burglary in SC carries a 15-year non-suspendable mandatory minimum — one of the harshest burglary penalties in the nation. Applies specifically to dwellings with aggravating circumstances. 'Dwelling' includes any structure used for habitation.

elements: Defendant entered a building or structure (not a dwelling) without consent
With the intent to commit a crime therein
enhancements: Two or more prior burglary convictions (up to 10 years under § 16-11-313(B))
notes: Third-degree burglary covers non-dwelling structures: businesses, warehouses, storage buildings, vehicles. Up to 5 years for first and second offense. Third offense escalates to 10-year maximum.

statute_title: Grand Larceny of a Motor Vehicle
elements: Defendant took a motor vehicle belonging to another
Without consent of the owner
With intent to permanently deprive the owner
notes: Motor vehicle theft is treated as grand larceny regardless of the vehicle's value. SC also criminalizes receiving stolen vehicles (§ 16-21-80) and altering VINs (§ 16-21-90).

elements: Defendant received, possessed, or acquired property
The property had been stolen
Defendant knew or had reason to believe the property was stolen
Defendant intended to deprive the rightful owner
notes: Same value thresholds as larceny: $2,000 for petit/grand distinction. Knowledge element can be proven by circumstantial evidence (price too good to be true, suspicious circumstances). Frequently charged alongside the underlying theft.

elements: Defendant willfully and maliciously damaged, destroyed, or defaced the property of another
Without the consent of the owner
enhancements: Damage to church, school, or public building
notes: SC's malicious injury statutes cover both personal property (§ 16-11-510) and real property (§ 16-11-520). Same felony threshold as larceny ($2,000). Restitution is standard. Also includes § 16-11-520 for damage to real property and § 16-11-535 for damage to public utilities.

statute_title: Trespassing / Entry on Lands of Another
elements: Defendant entered the lands or premises of another
After being given notice not to enter (posting, personal notice, or fencing)
Defendant did not have permission or lawful authority
enhancements: Trespassing with intent to commit a crime (may elevate to burglary)
notes: SC has multiple trespass statutes covering different situations: general trespass (§ 16-11-600), trespass after notice (§ 16-11-620), and entry on cultivated lands (§ 16-11-610). Posting signs constitutes constructive notice.

elements: Defendant willfully and maliciously cut, mutilated, defaced, or otherwise injured or destroyed personal property of another
notes: SC uses 'malicious injury to property' rather than 'criminal mischief.' Same statute as vandalism — § 16-11-510 covers personal property and § 16-11-520 covers real property.

elements: Defendant altered, transferred, or removed merchandise labels or price tags in a retail establishment
Defendant transferred merchandise between containers
Defendant concealed merchandise with intent to deprive the merchant
enhancements: Organized retail theft (multiple persons acting in concert)
notes: Charged under the same shoplifting statute (§ 16-13-110). Retail fraud in SC encompasses price tag switching, under-scanning, and organized retail theft rings.

statute_title: Domestic Violence — First Through Fourth Degree
offense_class: Misdemeanor (first/second/third degree); Felony (second degree with prior + first degree)
penalty_max: 30 days (third degree); 3 years (second degree); 10 years (first degree)
elements: Defendant caused physical harm or injury to a household member
A 'household member' includes spouses, former spouses, persons who have a child in common, or persons cohabitating or formerly cohabitating
Third degree: minor injury or threat of harm
Second degree: moderate bodily injury or violation of protective order
First degree: great bodily injury or use of deadly weapon or strangulation
enhancements: Prior DV conviction within 10 years (escalates degree)
Great bodily injury or weapon use (first degree — felony)
Third conviction of third-degree DV within 10 years elevates to second degree
notes: SC overhauled its DV laws in 2015 (Act 58). Four-degree system mirrors the A&B scheme. First offense third degree is a misdemeanor but repeat offenses escalate. Strangulation is automatically first degree. Mandatory arrest policy. Protective order violations are second degree.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (no prior DV); Felony (with prior DV conviction or great bodily injury)
elements: Defendant caused moderate bodily injury to a household member, OR
Defendant committed DV third degree while subject to a protective order, OR
Defendant has a prior DV conviction within 10 years
enhancements: Great bodily injury (elevates to first degree)
notes: SC's domestic battery equivalent. Second degree is the middle tier. 'Moderate bodily injury' requires medical treatment but is not life-threatening. Covered under the same comprehensive DV statute as domestic violence.

offense_class: Misdemeanor (minor neglect); Felony (if great bodily injury or death risk)
penalty_max: 30 days (minor); 10 years (great bodily harm or if child's life was endangered)
elements: Defendant had charge or custody of a child
Defendant willfully or unreasonably neglected the child
The neglect placed the child's life, health, or safety at unreasonable risk
notes: SC's child endangerment is charged under the Children's Code (Title 63). Covers scenarios from leaving a child unattended in a vehicle to exposing a child to drug manufacturing environments. Overlaps with DUI child endangerment (§ 56-5-2947) when alcohol/drugs are involved.

statute_title: Unlawful Conduct Toward a Child / Child Abuse
elements: Defendant had charge or custody of a child
Defendant placed the child at unreasonable risk of harm, OR willfully abandoned the child, OR
Defendant inflicted physical injury upon the child
enhancements: Sexual abuse (separate charges under sex offense statutes)
Child death resulting from abuse (homicide charges)
notes: SC addresses child abuse under Title 63 (Children's Code) and Title 16 (criminal law). Severe physical abuse may be charged as ABHAN or A&B in the first degree. DSS (Department of Social Services) investigation runs parallel to criminal proceedings.

elements: Defendant had charge, custody, or control of a child
Defendant failed to provide necessary care, supervision, food, clothing, shelter, or medical attention
The failure was willful or resulted from reckless disregard
enhancements: Great bodily injury or death of child
notes: Same statute as child endangerment (§ 63-5-70). SC does not sharply distinguish between neglect and endangerment — both fall under unlawful conduct toward a child. Severity of the penalty depends on the risk or harm to the child.

statute_title: Domestic Violence — Violation of Order of Protection
offense_class: Misdemeanor (civil contempt); Felony if physical harm occurs
penalty_max: 30 days (contempt); 3 years (DV second degree if harm caused); 5 years (assault during violation)
elements: A valid order of protection was in effect
Defendant had notice of the order
Defendant willfully violated a condition of the order
enhancements: Physical harm during violation (elevates to DV second degree)
Violation involving threat with a weapon
notes: Violation of a protective order while committing DV is automatically second-degree DV under the 2015 reform. Civil contempt for non-violent violations. Mandatory arrest if officer determines violation occurred. Protective orders issued under § 16-25-30.

elements: Defendant engaged in a pattern of conduct directed at a specific person
The pattern of conduct served no legitimate purpose
A reasonable person in the victim's position would feel fear
enhancements: Aggravated stalking (§ 16-3-1700(C) — with credible threat, violation of order, or prior conviction)
notes: SC enacted comprehensive stalking legislation. 'Pattern of conduct' requires two or more acts. Stalking a minor or stalking in violation of a protective order elevates to aggravated stalking.

elements: Defendant engaged in stalking as defined in § 16-3-1700(A)
With at least one aggravating circumstance: credible threat of death or serious bodily injury, violation of a restraining or protective order, or prior stalking conviction
enhancements: Violation of protective order during stalking
notes: Felony aggravated stalking carries up to 5 years. Electronic monitoring may be ordered as a condition of bond. SC also recognizes stalking as a basis for a restraining order (§ 16-3-1750).

elements: Defendant engaged in a pattern of intentional, substantial, and unreasonable intrusion into the private life of another
Using electronic communication or social media to harass, threaten, or intimidate
enhancements: Threats of violence through electronic means (may elevate to aggravated stalking)
notes: SC addresses cyberstalking within the broader harassment and stalking framework. Also covered by § 16-17-430 (harassment via phone/electronic device). Social media threats and cyberbullying of adults fall under these provisions.

elements: Defendant engaged in a pattern of intentional, substantial, and unreasonable intrusion into the private life of a targeted person
The conduct served no legitimate purpose
enhancements: Harassment in violation of protective order
notes: Harassment in SC is addressed under the same statute as stalking. Less severe than stalking (no fear requirement, just unreasonable intrusion). Telephone harassment is a separate misdemeanor under § 16-17-430.

statute_title: Abuse, Neglect, or Exploitation of a Vulnerable Adult
elements: Defendant committed an act of abuse, neglect, or exploitation against a vulnerable adult
A 'vulnerable adult' includes persons over 18 with physical or mental conditions that impair their ability to protect themselves
Defendant acted willfully or through reckless disregard
enhancements: Death of victim resulting from abuse/neglect
notes: SC's Omnibus Adult Protection Act (§ 43-35-10 et seq.) covers vulnerable adult abuse. Includes elderly persons and those with disabilities. Mandatory reporting requirements for certain professionals. Financial exploitation carries penalties based on amount taken.

statute_title: Financial Exploitation of a Vulnerable Adult
elements: Defendant was entrusted with or had access to the property or finances of a vulnerable adult
Defendant knowingly used, consumed, or disposed of the vulnerable adult's property or finances
Without the vulnerable adult's consent or through undue influence
notes: Financial exploitation is the most commonly prosecuted form of elder abuse in SC. Includes unauthorized use of POA, draining bank accounts, forging signatures, and predatory lending targeting vulnerable adults. Restitution is mandatory.

penalty_max: 1 year or $1,000 fine (first); 3 years or $2,000 fine (second+)
elements: Defendant carried a handgun about the person
Defendant was in a location where carrying was prohibited
Defendant did not have a valid concealed weapons permit (CWP) or was not exempt
enhancements: Carrying during commission of violent crime
notes: SC enacted open carry with training in 2024 (Act 135). CWP holders and open carriers with required training can carry in most public places. Prohibited locations include courthouses, police stations, churches (without permission), hospitals, schools, and government buildings. SC is not a permitless carry state — training is still required.

statute_title: Possession of a Firearm by a Person Convicted of a Crime of Violence
elements: Defendant possessed, owned, or had in their control a firearm (pistol or rifle)
Defendant had been previously convicted of a 'crime of violence' as defined in § 16-1-60
mandatory_minimum: 1 year (cannot be suspended to less than 1 year)
enhancements: Use of firearm during commission of another crime
notes: SC restricts this to persons convicted of 'crimes of violence' (§ 16-1-60) rather than all felons. Crimes of violence include murder, assault, robbery, burglary, kidnapping, arson, and other specified offenses. The 1-year minimum cannot be suspended. Also subject to federal felon-in-possession charges under 18 USC 922(g).

statute_title: Unlawful Carrying of a Concealed Weapon
elements: Defendant carried a concealed weapon about the person
Without a valid SC Concealed Weapons Permit or recognized out-of-state permit
Defendant was not otherwise exempt from the permit requirement
notes: SC recognizes concealed carry with a CWP and open carry with required training (as of 2024). Concealed carry without a permit remains illegal. SC has reciprocity with most states' CCW permits. Knives with blades over 2 inches are also covered.

statute_title: Pointing or Presenting a Firearm at Another / Discharging a Firearm
penalty_max: 5 years (pointing at a person); additional penalties for discharge
elements: Defendant pointed or presented a firearm at another person, OR
Defendant discharged a firearm in a manner endangering the life or safety of others
enhancements: Discharge into an occupied dwelling or vehicle (§ 16-23-440 — felony, up to 10 years)
notes: Pointing a firearm at another person is a standalone offense in SC. Discharging into an occupied building/vehicle is a separate, more serious felony under § 16-23-440. Random gunfire in populated areas can be charged under multiple statutes.

statute_title: Illegal Sale or Transfer of Firearms
elements: Defendant sold, offered to sell, or transferred a firearm to a person prohibited from possessing one
Defendant knew or had reason to know the recipient was prohibited
notes: SC restricts sales to convicted violent offenders and minors. Straw purchases are prosecuted federally. SC does not require private-sale background checks — federal law governs private sales.

statute_title: Unlawful Possession of a Sawed-Off Shotgun, Rifle, or Machine Gun
elements: Defendant possessed, sold, or transported a sawed-off shotgun (barrel <18 inches), sawed-off rifle (barrel <16 inches), or machine gun
Without lawful authority under the National Firearms Act
enhancements: Use during commission of a violent crime
notes: SC prohibits sawed-off shotguns, sawed-off rifles, and machine guns absent NFA compliance. Silencers are legal in SC with proper ATF registration. The 2-year mandatory minimum is non-suspendable.

elements: Defendant carried a weapon about the person
In a manner or location prohibited by law
Without a valid permit or exemption
enhancements: Carrying in a prohibited location (courthouse, school, etc.)
notes: Covers handguns and knives with blades over 2 inches. Post-2024 open carry reform changed the landscape — open carry with training is now legal in most public places. Prohibited locations remain strict.

statute_title: Use of a Firearm During Commission of a Violent Crime
elements: Defendant was in possession of a firearm during the commission of a violent crime
The underlying offense was a crime of violence as defined in § 16-1-60
mandatory_minimum: 5 years (consecutive, non-suspendable, no probation or parole)
notes: This is an additional consecutive sentence on top of the underlying crime. The 5-year mandatory minimum cannot be suspended and must be served consecutively with any other sentence. Applies to any 'crime of violence' under SC law.

statute_title: Carrying a Weapon in a Prohibited Location
elements: Defendant carried a weapon into a prohibited location
Prohibited locations include: courthouses, police stations, schools, churches (without express permission), government buildings, hospitals, and posted private property
enhancements: Carrying in a school (separate offense under § 16-23-430 — up to 5 years)
notes: Even CWP holders and open carriers cannot carry in prohibited locations. § 16-23-420 lists specific prohibited places. Church carry requires express permission of the church leadership. Private businesses can prohibit firearms with proper signage.

statute_title: Possession of a Firearm on School Property
elements: Defendant possessed a firearm or destructive device on school property
School property includes school buildings, grounds, school buses, and school-sponsored events
enhancements: Use or brandishing of firearm on school grounds
notes: Applies to all persons, including CWP holders. Separate from the federal Gun-Free School Zones Act. Includes all school property, school buses, and school events. Exceptions for law enforcement and authorized school personnel.

statute_title: Illegal Possession of Explosives or Incendiary Devices
elements: Defendant possessed, manufactured, transported, or distributed an explosive or incendiary device
With the intent to cause harm or without lawful authority
enhancements: Possession near a public building or school
notes: SC's Destructive Device Act covers bombs, grenades, and incendiary devices. Legitimate commercial explosives users must be licensed. Also subject to federal ATF regulations.

elements: Defendant used or possessed the personal identifying information of another person
Without that person's consent
With intent to commit or facilitate a crime
enhancements: Victim is a vulnerable adult or minor
notes: SC's Financial Identity Fraud and Identity Theft Protection Act (§ 16-13-500 et seq.) is comprehensive. Covers use of names, SSNs, account numbers, passwords. Victims have right to expedited investigation. Identity theft of deceased persons also covered.

statute_title: Breach of Trust With Fraudulent Intent
elements: Defendant was entrusted with property or funds by another
Defendant converted the property or funds to personal use
With fraudulent intent
notes: SC calls embezzlement 'breach of trust with fraudulent intent.' Same value thresholds as larceny. Public official embezzlement may also be charged under § 16-13-240. Restitution is standard.

elements: Defendant falsely made, forged, or altered a writing or document
The document would have legal efficacy if genuine
With intent to defraud
enhancements: Forging public records or government documents
notes: SC forgery statute covers checks, deeds, contracts, and other legal documents. Uttering a forged instrument (presenting it as genuine) is charged under the same statute. Each forged document may be a separate count.

statute_title: Counterfeiting — Possession or Use of Counterfeit Bills
elements: Defendant knowingly possessed, used, or passed counterfeit currency or financial instruments
With intent to defraud
notes: Most counterfeiting cases are prosecuted federally (18 USC 471-474). SC statute covers state-level counterfeiting of various instruments. Federal Secret Service typically investigates counterfeit currency cases.

elements: Defendant drew, uttered, or delivered a check, draft, or order
On any bank or depository for payment of money
Knowing at the time that the account had insufficient funds
With intent to defraud the payee
notes: SC uses lower thresholds for bad checks than for larceny ($1,000 vs. $2,000 for felony). Failure to make good within 15 days of notice creates a rebuttable presumption of intent to defraud. Restitution is standard.

elements: Defendant willfully attempted to evade or defeat a tax imposed by the SC tax code
By filing a fraudulent return, failing to file a return, or underreporting income
enhancements: Pattern of evasion over multiple years
notes: SC Department of Revenue investigates state tax fraud. Federal tax evasion is separate. SC imposes both criminal penalties and civil fraud penalties (up to 75% of underpayment). Voluntary disclosure program may reduce criminal exposure.

elements: Defendant knowingly presented or caused to be presented a false or fraudulent insurance claim
For payment or benefit under an insurance policy
With intent to defraud
notes: SC Insurance Fraud and Reporting Immunity Act. Covers auto insurance fraud, health insurance fraud, property insurance claims fraud. SC Department of Insurance has a fraud division. Arson for insurance fraud is separately charged under arson statutes.

statute_title: Fraudulent Use of Credit Card / Financial Transaction Card Fraud
offense_class: Misdemeanor ($500 or less in 6 months); Felony (over $500 in 6 months)
elements: Defendant used a credit card, debit card, or financial transaction card
The card was stolen, forged, expired, revoked, or not the defendant's
Defendant knew the card was unauthorized
With intent to defraud
enhancements: Total fraud exceeds $500 in a 6-month period (felony)
Use of skimming or cloning devices
notes: SC Financial Transaction Card Crime Act (§ 16-14-10 et seq.) is comprehensive. Covers card theft, counterfeiting, and fraudulent use. The $500 threshold is calculated over any 6-month period. Manufacturing card reading/writing devices is a separate felony.

elements: Defendant conducted or attempted to conduct a financial transaction
Involving proceeds of unlawful activity
With knowledge that the transaction was designed to conceal the nature, location, source, ownership, or control of the proceeds
enhancements: Structuring transactions to avoid reporting requirements
notes: SC money laundering statute (§ 16-13-530) is modeled on federal law. Often charged alongside drug trafficking. Financial institutions must file Suspicious Activity Reports. State and federal charges may be brought simultaneously.

statute_title: Obtaining Property or Signature Under False Pretenses
elements: Defendant made a false pretense or representation of a material fact
With intent to defraud another person
The victim relied on the false pretense
As a result, the victim parted with property or something of value
notes: SC's general fraud statute — 'obtaining goods under false pretenses.' Same value thresholds as larceny. Covers a wide range of fraudulent schemes. Each transaction may be a separate count.

elements: Defendant knowingly made or caused to be made a false statement or representation of material fact
In applying for or determining rights to Medicaid or healthcare benefits
With intent to defraud
enhancements: Patient harm resulting from fraudulent care
notes: SC Attorney General's Medicaid Fraud Control Unit investigates. Covers billing fraud, kickbacks, and patient abuse in Medicaid-funded facilities. Federal healthcare fraud charges may also apply (18 USC 1347).

elements: Defendant made a material misrepresentation or omission in a mortgage loan application or transaction
With intent to defraud the lender, borrower, or a third party
notes: SC enacted specific mortgage fraud provisions. Also prosecuted under the general false pretenses statute. Federal charges common in major mortgage fraud cases. SC Consumer Protection Code (Title 37) provides additional civil remedies.

elements: Defendant obtained public assistance benefits by fraud, misrepresentation, or failure to disclose material information
Defendant was not entitled to the benefits received
enhancements: Pattern of fraud over extended period
notes: Covers SNAP (food stamps), TANF, Medicaid eligibility fraud, and other public assistance programs. DSS refers cases for prosecution. Restitution plus disqualification from benefits.

elements: Defendant willfully, knowingly, and without authorization accessed or caused to be accessed a computer, computer system, or computer network
With intent to deceive, defraud, obtain money or property, or cause disruption
enhancements: Damage exceeding $10,000 (first degree — up to 10 years)
Data breach affecting large numbers of persons
notes: SC Computer Crime Act (§ 16-16-10 et seq.) classifies computer crimes by degree. Covers hacking, ransomware, data theft, and unauthorized access. Three degrees: first (most serious, affecting commerce/government), second, and third. SC also has data breach notification requirements (§ 39-1-90).

elements: Defendant engaged in sexual battery (sexual intercourse, cunnilingus, fellatio, anal intercourse, or intrusion) with the victim
Force or coercion was used to accomplish the act, OR
The victim was mentally or physically incapacitated
notes: SC uses the Criminal Sexual Conduct (CSC) framework with three degrees plus criminal sexual conduct with a minor. Third degree is the base-level felony sexual offense involving sexual battery. No parole for CSC convictions — sentence must be served day-for-day under the 85% rule.

elements: Defendant engaged in sexual battery with the victim
Through use of aggravated force, aggravated coercion, or when the victim was incapable of consent
enhancements: Aggravating circumstances (elevates to second or first degree)
notes: SC's 'sexual assault' is charged as CSC in the third degree. The CSC framework replaced common-law rape. Third degree covers sexual battery with force or coercion. More serious circumstances trigger first or second degree.

elements: Defendant engaged in sexual battery with the victim
With aggravated force (use of a weapon, threat of great bodily injury, or kidnapping), OR
Victim was physically helpless, OR
Defendant used aggravated coercion
enhancements: Victim under 11 years old (mandatory 25 years to life under § 16-3-655)
notes: First-degree CSC is the most serious sexual offense in SC. No parole eligibility. Must serve 85% of sentence before release eligibility. Sex offender registration required for life. If victim is under 11, mandatory minimum 25 years under § 16-3-655.

elements: Defendant engaged in sexual battery with the victim
Using aggravated coercion to accomplish the act, OR
Victim was mentally incapacitated, physically helpless, or had a mental disability
Without the aggravated force elements of first degree
notes: Second-degree CSC sits between first and third degree. Covers situations involving coercion, incapacitation, or abuse of a position of authority over the victim. No parole — 85% rule applies.

elements: Defendant engaged in sexual battery with the victim
Through the use of force or coercion (without aggravating factors of first or second degree), OR
Defendant knew or should have known that the victim was mentally defective, mentally incapacitated, or physically helpless
notes: Third-degree is the lowest CSC felony. Still carries sex offender registration. 85% of sentence must be served. Can be a lesser-included offense of first or second degree CSC.

statute_title: Criminal Sexual Conduct With a Minor — Third Degree
elements: Defendant engaged in sexual battery with a victim aged 14-15
Defendant was in a position of familial, custodial, or official authority, OR
Defendant was older than the victim by a specified number of years
notes: SC does not have a 'fourth degree' CSC in the same sense as Michigan. This entry maps to the least serious CSC-minor charge. SC's CSC-minor statute (§ 16-3-655) has three degrees based on victim age: first degree (under 11), second degree (11-14), third degree (14-15 with authority relationship).

statute_title: Criminal Sexual Conduct — First Degree (Forcible Rape)
elements: Defendant engaged in non-consensual sexual battery with the victim
Through use of aggravated force, threats of death or serious bodily injury
Victim was unable to consent due to force, coercion, or incapacity
enhancements: Victim under 11 years old (25 years to life)
notes: SC abolished the common-law crime of rape and replaced it with the CSC framework. What was traditionally 'rape' is now CSC in the first degree. No statute of limitations for CSC first degree.

statute_title: Criminal Sexual Conduct With a Minor
elements: Defendant engaged in sexual battery with a minor
First degree: victim under 11; Second degree: victim 11-14 and defendant at least 3 years older; Third degree: victim 14-15 and defendant in authority or older
enhancements: Defendant was caretaker or authority figure
notes: SC's age of consent is 16. CSC with a minor has three degrees based on victim age. No statute of limitations for CSC with a minor first degree (victim under 11). Jessica's Law equivalent: mandatory 25 years for sexual battery of a child under 11.

statute_title: Criminal Sexual Conduct — Third Degree (Sexual Battery)
elements: Defendant engaged in sexual battery (defined as sexual intercourse, cunnilingus, fellatio, anal intercourse, or any intrusion of any body part or object into genital or anal openings) with the victim
Through force, coercion, or without consent
notes: SC defines 'sexual battery' broadly to include all forms of sexual penetration and intrusion. This is the base sexual offense. Aggravating factors elevate to second or first degree. Sex offender registration required.

elements: Defendant willfully and maliciously exposed private parts in a public place or in view of the public
In a lewd and lascivious manner
enhancements: Exposure in the presence of a minor
notes: Indecent exposure can trigger sex offender registration if the court finds a sexual motivation or if the victim is a minor. Charged under § 16-15-130 (Indecent Exposure) which carries up to 3 years. Breastfeeding in public is explicitly exempt.

elements: Defendant solicited or procured another for the purpose of prostitution
Or offered to engage in prostitution
enhancements: Third or subsequent offense (up to 1 year)
Soliciting a minor for prostitution (felony under human trafficking statutes)
notes: SC criminalizes both the buyer and seller in prostitution. Solicitation of a minor triggers human trafficking charges under § 16-3-2020. John school or diversion programs may be available for first offenders in some jurisdictions.

elements: Defendant engaged in, offered to engage in, or agreed to engage in sexual activity for money or other consideration
notes: Same statute as solicitation. SC does not have a safe harbor law shielding trafficking victims from prostitution charges, though prosecutorial discretion is often applied. Keeping a house of prostitution is a separate offense under § 16-15-100.

statute_title: Keeping a House of Prostitution / Pandering
elements: Defendant maintained, controlled, or managed a place for the purpose of prostitution, lewdness, or assignation, OR
Defendant procured or induced another to enter or leave a place for prostitution
enhancements: Pandering involving minors (felony under trafficking statutes)
notes: Covers brothel keeping, pimping, and pandering. When minors are involved, charges escalate to human trafficking under § 16-3-2020 with much harsher penalties.

statute_title: Criminal Solicitation of a Minor / Online Sexual Offense
elements: Defendant used a computer, internet, or electronic device to solicit, entice, or lure a minor
For the purpose of engaging in sexual activity
Or to produce sexual material involving the minor
enhancements: Traveling to meet the minor after online solicitation
Distribution of obscene material to the minor
notes: SC has specific online predator statutes. § 16-15-342 criminalizes online solicitation of minors. Also covers adults posing as minors online. Law enforcement sting operations are common and admissible.

statute_title: Sexual Exploitation of a Minor — First/Second/Third Degree
penalty_max: 20 years (first degree); 10 years (second degree); 10 years (third degree)
elements: First degree: defendant used, employed, induced, or permitted a minor to engage in sexual activity for visual representation
Second degree: defendant recorded, photographed, or distributed visual representation of a minor engaged in sexual activity
Third degree: defendant possessed material containing visual representation of a minor in sexual activity
notes: SC has a three-degree system for child exploitation offenses. First degree (production) is most serious at up to 20 years. Mandatory sex offender registration. Mandatory minimum of 2 years even for possession (third degree). No statute of limitations.

statute_title: Third Degree Sexual Exploitation of a Minor (Possession of Child Pornography)
elements: Defendant knowingly possessed material that contained a visual representation of a minor engaging in sexual activity
enhancements: Multiple images (each image may be a separate count)
notes: Each item of child pornography can be a separate count. The 2-year mandatory minimum applies per conviction. Sex offender registration required for life. Federal charges under 18 USC 2252 may also apply, carrying heavier penalties.

statute_title: First Degree Sexual Exploitation of a Minor (Production)
elements: Defendant used, employed, induced, coerced, or permitted a minor to engage in sexual activity for a visual representation
Defendant produced, directed, or promoted the visual representation
notes: Production is the most severely punished child exploitation offense in SC. Each visual representation is a separate count. Typically also triggers federal charges with even longer mandatory minimums (15-30 years under 18 USC 2251).

statute_title: Failure to Register as Sex Offender
elements: Defendant was required to register as a sex offender under the SC Sex Offender Registry Act
Defendant failed to register, update registration, or provide required information within the specified time period
enhancements: Second or subsequent failure (up to 10 years)
notes: SC Sex Offender Registry Act (§ 23-3-400 et seq.) requires registration within 3 business days of establishing residence, employment, or enrollment in school. Must update annually (or quarterly for certain offenders). Lifetime registration for most sex offenses.

elements: Defendant recruited, enticed, harbored, transported, provided, or obtained a person
For the purpose of forced labor or commercial sexual activity
Through force, fraud, or coercion
notes: SC's human trafficking statute carries a 15-year mandatory minimum — one of the harshest in the nation. Trafficking of a minor does not require proof of force, fraud, or coercion. Victims may receive restitution and have access to victim services. Asset forfeiture applies.

elements: Defendant was found in a public place or gathering in a grossly intoxicated condition, OR
Defendant used obscene or profane language in a public place or gathering, OR
Defendant engaged in conduct that was of a nature to provoke others to breach of the peace
notes: SC's disorderly conduct statute is relatively narrow. Often charged alongside other public order offenses. First Amendment protections apply — mere profanity without a threat or incitement may be protected speech.

elements: A law enforcement officer was making a lawful arrest
Defendant knew or should have known the officer was performing official duties
Defendant resisted the arrest by force or by fleeing
enhancements: Causing bodily injury to officer during resistance (may elevate to A&B on law enforcement)
notes: SC requires the underlying arrest to be lawful. An unlawful arrest cannot support a resisting charge. Passive resistance (going limp) is generally not sufficient. Physical resistance or active flight is required.

elements: Defendant willfully hindered, delayed, or obstructed a law enforcement officer, judicial officer, or magistrate
In the discharge of their official duties
By threat, assault, or other unlawful means
enhancements: Violence or threats against officer or official
notes: SC obstruction can be charged as either misdemeanor or felony depending on the nature of the obstruction. Destroying evidence, giving false testimony, or hiding a fugitive all qualify. Separate from resisting arrest.

penalty_max: 1 year (criminal contempt); indefinite (civil contempt — purge condition)
elements: A valid court order was in effect
Defendant had knowledge of the order
Defendant willfully disobeyed the order
notes: Civil contempt is coercive (designed to compel compliance) and ends when defendant complies. Criminal contempt is punitive. Family court contempt is common for failure to pay child support. Defendant is entitled to a hearing.

elements: Defendant committed behavior that was contemptuous of court authority
The behavior was willful
The contempt was punishable as a criminal offense (beyond civil coercion)
notes: Criminal contempt in SC is limited to 1 year by statute. Anything beyond that requires a jury trial. Direct contempt (in the courtroom) can be punished summarily. Indirect contempt (outside the courtroom) requires notice and a hearing.

elements: Defendant lingered, remained, or prowled in a public place
Under circumstances that warranted alarm for the safety of persons or property in the vicinity
Defendant failed to identify themselves and explain their presence when requested by law enforcement
notes: SC loitering statutes have been narrowed by court challenges. Many localities have their own loitering ordinances. Must be careful not to violate constitutional vagueness and overbreadth doctrines.

elements: Defendant engaged in conduct that unreasonably disturbed the public peace
In a public place or gathering
notes: Covered under the same disorderly conduct statute. SC does not have a separate 'disturbing the peace' statute — the conduct is charged under § 16-17-530 disorderly conduct.

statute_title: Failure to Appear / Forfeiture of Bond
penalty_max: 5 years (felony charge FTA); 1 year (misdemeanor charge FTA)
elements: Defendant was released on bail or recognizance
Defendant was required to appear at a specific court date and time
Defendant willfully failed to appear
notes: Failure to appear triggers bond forfeiture and a separate criminal charge. Severity depends on the underlying charge. A bench warrant is issued immediately. FTA on a felony is itself a felony. Bondsman has 60 days to surrender defendant before full forfeiture.

elements: Defendant made a statement to a law enforcement officer
The statement concerned a crime or potential crime
The statement was knowingly false
enhancements: False report that results in wrongful arrest or prosecution
notes: Relatively minor penalty for filing a false report. However, if the false report targets a specific person, additional charges (harassment, conspiracy, perjury) may apply. Swatting (false emergency reports) may also trigger federal charges.

statute_title: Criminal Threats / Assault (Threat of Bodily Harm)
penalty_max: 1 year (general threat); up to 5 years (threat against public official)
elements: Defendant made a threat to cause bodily harm to another person
The threat was made willfully and with apparent ability to carry it out
A reasonable person would have perceived the threat as genuine
notes: SC addresses criminal threats through multiple statutes depending on the target and context. General threats of violence may be charged as assault (threat component of A&B third degree). Threats against specific classes of persons carry enhanced penalties.

elements: Defendant was under oath or affirmation in a judicial proceeding or before a competent officer
Defendant made a material false statement
Defendant knew the statement was false
enhancements: Subornation of perjury (inducing another to commit perjury — same penalty)
notes: Perjury in SC requires that the statement be material to the proceeding. Contradictory sworn statements may constitute perjury even without independent proof of which was false. Subornation of perjury (§ 16-9-20) carries the same penalty.

elements: Defendant offered, gave, or promised something of value to a public official, juror, or witness
With the intent to influence their official action, vote, opinion, or testimony
enhancements: Bribery of a judge (enhanced under separate statute)
notes: SC bribery statutes cover both the giver and receiver of the bribe. § 16-9-210 covers bribery of public officials. § 16-9-220 covers bribery of jurors. Separate statutes for bribery in athletic contests (§ 16-9-250).

statute_title: Witness Tampering / Intimidation of a Witness
elements: Defendant corruptly influenced, intimidated, or threatened a witness or potential witness
With the intent to influence their testimony or prevent them from testifying
enhancements: Use of physical violence or threats of violence
Witness tampering in a capital case
notes: Witness tampering is a serious obstruction charge. Includes bribing witnesses, threatening witnesses, or persuading witnesses to provide false testimony. Often charged alongside the underlying case when discovered.

statute_title: Bribery of a Juror / Jury Tampering
elements: Defendant offered, gave, or promised something of value to a juror or potential juror
With the intent to influence the juror's vote, deliberation, or verdict
notes: Jury tampering includes any improper contact with a juror designed to influence the outcome. Both the person making the offer and the juror who accepts are culpable.

elements: Defendant was in lawful custody (prison, jail, or during transport)
Defendant escaped or attempted to escape from that custody
enhancements: Use of force or violence during escape
Escape while awaiting trial for a violent felony
notes: Sentence for escape is served consecutive to any existing sentence. Escape from local detention is § 16-9-340. Walking away from work release or minimum-security facilities also qualifies. Failure to return from furlough is a separate offense.

elements: Defendant falsely represented themselves as a law enforcement officer
By wearing a uniform, displaying a badge, or claiming to be an officer
With the intent to deceive others
enhancements: Committing a crime while impersonating (additional charges)
notes: Includes wearing police-style uniforms, using flashing blue lights, or displaying fake credentials. Using impersonation to commit another crime (robbery, sexual assault) results in additional charges.

statute_title: Penalty Enhancement — Offense Motivated by Bias
penalty_max: Enhancement adds up to 5 years to underlying offense
elements: Defendant committed an underlying criminal offense
The offense was motivated in whole or in part by bias based on the victim's race, color, religion, sex, gender, national origin, sexual orientation, or physical/mental disability
notes: SC enacted its hate crime law in 2023 (Clementa C. Pinckney Hate Crimes Act). Named after the state senator killed in the 2015 Emanuel AME Church shooting. This was one of the last states to add hate crime legislation. Enhances the penalty of the underlying offense.

elements: Defendant participated in a criminal street gang
Defendant committed or conspired to commit a predicate offense for the benefit of or at the direction of the gang
enhancements: Recruitment of a minor into a gang
notes: SC Criminal Gang Prevention Act (§ 16-8-210 et seq.). 'Criminal street gang' requires three or more members and an ongoing pattern of criminal activity. Gang-motivated offenses carry enhanced penalties. Asset forfeiture applies to gang-related property.

elements: Defendant used electronic communications to repeatedly harass, intimidate, or threaten another person
The conduct served no legitimate purpose
A reasonable person would suffer emotional distress from the conduct
enhancements: Threats of violence (may elevate to aggravated stalking)
notes: Cyberbullying of minors is also addressed by school disciplinary policies and § 59-63-120. Adult cyberbullying is charged under the harassment and stalking statutes. Social media platforms may be subpoenaed for evidence.

elements: Defendant intentionally or knowingly tortured, tormented, needlessly mutilated, cruelly killed, or inflicted excessive or repeated unnecessary pain or suffering upon an animal, OR
Defendant failed to provide an animal with necessary sustenance
enhancements: Animal fighting (§ 16-17-650 — felony, up to 5 years)
notes: SC animal cruelty law was strengthened in 2000. Aggravated cruelty (torture) is a felony. Animal fighting (dogfighting, cockfighting) is a separate felony. Mandatory counseling may be ordered. Courts can order forfeiture of animals.

statute_title: Threatening to Use a Destructive Device / Bomb Threat
elements: Defendant threatened to use or cause to be placed a destructive device or explosive
In or near a public building, school, church, or other structure
The threat was made willfully and with intent to cause alarm
notes: Bomb threats are taken very seriously in SC. Prosecution does not require that a real device exists. Hoax devices are also criminal. Federal charges may apply for threats against federal buildings or using interstate communications.

elements: Defendant subjected another person to physical or psychological abuse
As part of an initiation, admission, or affiliation with an organization
The conduct was intentional
enhancements: Serious bodily injury resulting from hazing
Death resulting from hazing (manslaughter or murder charges may apply)
notes: SC hazing statute applies to fraternities, sororities, and other organizations. Consent of the victim is not a defense. Schools and universities are also required to have anti-hazing policies. Death resulting from hazing may trigger involuntary manslaughter charges.

elements: Defendant created or allowed excessive noise in violation of a local noise ordinance
The noise exceeded the level permitted for the time and location
notes: SC does not have a statewide noise ordinance — noise violations are governed by municipal and county ordinances. Common in Charleston, Columbia, Greenville, and Myrtle Beach. May also be charged under disorderly conduct (§ 16-17-530) for extreme noise.

elements: Defendant disposed of waste, garbage, or other materials
In a location not designated for disposal
Without authorization
notes: General littering is under SC Litter Control Act (§ 44-67-10 et seq.). Hazardous waste dumping is a felony under the SC Hazardous Waste Management Act. DHEC (Department of Health and Environmental Control) is the enforcement agency.

penalty_max: Up to the maximum sentence for the original offense
elements: Defendant was placed on probation by a court
Defendant violated one or more conditions of probation
The violation was willful and substantial
enhancements: Commission of a new crime while on probation (substantive violation)
notes: Probation revocation in SC requires a hearing. The court may revoke probation and impose any sentence that could have been imposed originally. Graduated sanctions (SC Omnibus Crime Reduction and Sentencing Reform Act of 2010) allow for intermediate sanctions before full revocation.

penalty_max: Graduated sanctions; up to original maximum if revoked
elements: Defendant was on probation supervision
Defendant violated a non-criminal condition of probation (missed check-in, failed drug test, missed curfew, etc.)
notes: SC's 2010 Omnibus Crime Reduction Act requires graduated sanctions for technical violations before full revocation. Administrative sanctions include increased reporting, community service, GPS monitoring, and short jail stays. Full revocation hearing required if sanctions fail.

penalty_max: Up to the maximum sentence for the original offense, served consecutively with new charge
