elements: Defendant was on probation supervision
Defendant committed a new criminal offense while on probation
enhancements: New drug offense while on probation for drug offense
notes: Substantive violations allow the court to revoke probation and impose the full original sentence. The new charge and revoked sentence may be served consecutively. Graduated sanctions do not apply to substantive violations.

offense_class: Varies (return to prison for remaining sentence)
elements: Defendant was released on parole
Defendant violated one or more conditions of parole
The SC Department of Probation, Parole, and Pardon Services (DPPPS) initiated revocation
enhancements: Commission of new crime while on parole
notes: Parole revocation is handled by the SC Board of Paroles and Pardons (SCDPPPS). A revocation hearing is required. If revoked, the parolee returns to prison for the remaining sentence. SC has reduced parole use since truth-in-sentencing reforms — most sentences now require serving 85% before parole eligibility.

penalty_max: Up to the maximum sentence for the original offense
elements: Defendant was placed on home detention or electronic monitoring as a condition of supervision
Defendant violated the terms by leaving the approved area, tampering with the device, or other violation
notes: SC uses home detention and GPS monitoring as alternatives to incarceration and as probation conditions. Tampering with monitoring equipment is a separate criminal offense. Violations are handled through the probation revocation process.

offense_class: Felony (if underlying offense is felony); Misdemeanor (if underlying offense is misdemeanor)
elements: An agreement existed between two or more persons to commit a criminal offense
Defendant knowingly and voluntarily entered the agreement
At least one overt act was committed in furtherance of the conspiracy
enhancements: Conspiracy to commit a violent crime
Drug conspiracy (triggers drug trafficking mandatory minimums)
notes: SC's general conspiracy statute (§ 16-17-410). Conspiracy is punished up to 5 years for felony conspiracy — may be less than the underlying offense. Drug conspiracy under § 44-53-403 carries the same penalties as the underlying drug offense, which may be harsher.

elements: Defendant recruited, enticed, solicited, isolated, harbored, transported, provided, obtained, or maintained a person
For the purpose of forced labor or commercial sexual exploitation
Through force, fraud, or coercion (not required for victims under 18)
enhancements: Victim under 18 (no proof of force/fraud/coercion needed)
notes: SC's trafficking statute is one of the most comprehensive in the nation. The 15-year mandatory minimum for sex trafficking is among the harshest. Asset forfeiture, restitution, and victim services are mandatory. SC also has an affirmative defense for trafficking victims charged with prostitution.

elements: Defendant was a public official or employee
Defendant used their office for personal gain, accepted bribes, or committed fraud in the exercise of official duties
notes: SC Ethics Act (§ 8-13-100 et seq.) governs public official conduct. State Ethics Commission investigates. Criminal prosecution handled by the Attorney General or solicitor. The State Grand Jury has jurisdiction over public corruption cases (§ 14-7-1610).

elements: Defendant knowingly treated, stored, disposed of, transported, or caused to be transported hazardous waste in violation of the SC Hazardous Waste Management Act
Without required permits or in violation of permit conditions
enhancements: Knowing endangerment (risk of death or serious bodily injury)
notes: SC DHEC (Department of Health and Environmental Control) is the primary enforcement agency. Also covers illegal discharge into waterways (Clean Water Act), air quality violations, and asbestos violations. Federal EPA may pursue parallel enforcement.

statute_title: Protection of Persons and Property (Stand Your Ground / Castle Doctrine)
offense_class: Affirmative Defense (not a charge — defense to prosecution)
elements: Defendant reasonably believed that deadly force was necessary to prevent imminent death or great bodily injury
Defendant was in a place where they had a right to be
Defendant was not engaged in unlawful activity
No duty to retreat exists in any place where the defendant has a legal right to be (Stand Your Ground)
notes: SC enacted its Protection of Persons and Property Act in 2006 (§ 16-11-440). Strong Stand Your Ground law — no duty to retreat in any place defendant has a right to be. Castle Doctrine provides presumption of reasonable fear in the home. Immunity hearing available pre-trial — if granted, defendant is immune from prosecution. Civil immunity also applies.

statute_title: Aiding and Abetting / Accessory Before the Fact
elements: A criminal offense was committed by the principal
Defendant counseled, aided, abetted, or procured the commission of the offense
Defendant intended to promote or assist in the commission of the offense
notes: SC treats aiders and abettors the same as principals (§ 16-1-40). An accessory before the fact is punishable as if they were the principal. An accessory after the fact (§ 16-1-50) is a separate, lesser offense. SC has abolished the common-law distinction between accessory and principal for most purposes.

offense_class: Varies (generally lesser penalty than completed offense)
penalty_max: Generally one-half the maximum penalty for the completed offense; specific attempt statutes may vary
elements: Defendant intended to commit a specific criminal offense
Defendant took a direct action beyond mere preparation toward completing the offense
The offense was not completed
enhancements: Attempted murder has its own specific statute (§ 16-3-29) with up to 30 years
notes: SC's general attempt statute applies when there is no specific attempt statute for the offense. Some offenses have specific attempt statutes with defined penalties (e.g., attempted murder § 16-3-29). The general rule is that attempt carries up to one-half the penalty of the completed offense.

elements: Elements vary depending on the specific offense charged
notes: Catch-all for SC criminal offenses not covered by specific categories. SC criminal code is Title 16. Additional criminal provisions exist throughout the SC Code of Laws (e.g., Title 44 for drug offenses, Title 56 for traffic offenses, Title 63 for children's code offenses).
